subtheme: Making distributed learning faster and fairer

subsubthemes.name: Handling uneven data across workers
subsubthemes.gist: When different machines have different types of data (called non-IID data), the learning goes slower and less accurately; these papers find ways to make it work anyway.

subsubthemes.name: Cutting communication costs between machines
subsubthemes.gist: Sending updates between machines is slow and expensive; these papers find ways to compress or reduce the amount of information that needs to be sent.

subsubthemes.name: Making federated learning prove its convergence
subsubthemes.gist: Researchers need to show mathematically that federated algorithms actually reach good solutions, especially when data is uneven and noisy across machines.

subsubthemes.name: Keeping learning stable when workers fail
subsubthemes.gist: In distributed learning, some machines may crash or behave badly; these papers develop ways to keep training working reliably even when things go wrong.

subsubthemes.name: Making optimization algorithms faster
subsubthemes.gist: Standard gradient descent can be slow; these papers adapt proven fast techniques like acceleration, momentum, and second-order methods to distributed settings.

subsubthemes.name: Understanding what makes distributed algorithms work
subsubthemes.gist: Researchers analyze why distributed methods converge at all, what properties of the network and algorithm design matter most, and how they interact.

subsubthemes.name: Learning with multiple objectives or constraints
subsubthemes.gist: Real problems often have multiple goals to optimize at once or constraints to satisfy; these papers extend distributed methods to handle such complex scenarios.
